Agents ask about things that changed last week. If search hands back last month's answer, the agent repeats it with confidence.
Nitya Sridhar at Exa wrote that retrieval beyond model memory needs a specific focus on what is recent. So I tested exactly that.
I built fifty-eight queries whose answer changed in the last thirty days: new releases, prices, new CEOs, playoff results, and API deprecations. Each has a dated answer and a source.
Nineteen of them are held out, frozen by hash before a single call.
I ran them against Exa search on October fourteenth, across seven settings from instant to max age zero. Three hundred sixty-one calls, about two dollars and forty cents.
The result is mostly good news. Without a date filter, the current answer was in the top ten for nearly every query, and ranked first up to ninety-five percent of the time.
The date filter made results more precise, but it dropped undated official pages, so releases from that same morning were missed.
Max age zero gave the best top result, at about ten seconds a call. Instant and fast came back in under half a second.
Every check is code, validated against five hundred fifty-one hand labels. The data, cache, and harness are open, and anyone can rescore them without a key.
